cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: OK, Jack.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: Before we plan our presentation about refrigeration, let's discuss what we've discovered

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: so far.

cues.speaker: CK
cues.text: Fine, Annie. Though I have to admit I haven't done much research yet.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: Nor me. But I found an interesting article about icehouses.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: I'd been some 18th- and 19th-century ones here in the UK, so I knew they were often built

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: in a shady area or underground, close to lakes that might freeze in the winter.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: Then blocks of ice could be cut and stored in the icehouse.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: But I didn't realise that insulating the blocks with straw or sawdust meant they didn't

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: melt for months. The ancient Romans had refrigeration, too.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: Yes, pits were dug in the ground, and snow was imported from the mountains – even though

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: they were at quite a distance. The snow was stored in the pits.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: Ice formed at the bottom of it. Both the ice and the snow were then sold.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: The ice cost more than the snow and my guess is that only the wealthy members of society

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: could afford it.

cues.speaker: CK
cues.text: I wouldn't be surprised. I also came across an article about modern domestic fridges.

cues.speaker: CK
cues.text: Several different technologies are used, but they were too complex for me to understand.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: You have to wonder what happens when people get rid of old ones.

cues.speaker: CK
cues.text: You mean because the gases in them are harmful for the environment?

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: Exactly.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: At least these are now plenty of organisations that will recycle most of the components

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: safety, but of course some people just dump old fridges in the countryside.

cues.speaker: CK
cues.text: It's hard to see how they can be stopped unfortunately.

cues.speaker: CK
cues.text: In the UK we get rid of three million a year altogether!

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: That sounds a lot, especially because fridges hardly ever break down.

cues.speaker: CK
cues.text: That's right.

cues.speaker: CK
cues.text: In this country we keep domestic fridges for 11 years on average, and a lot last for 20

cues.speaker: CK
cues.text: or more.

cues.speaker: CK
cues.text: So if you divide the cost by the number of years you can use a fridge, they're not

cues.speaker: CK
cues.text: expensive, compared with some household appliances.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: True.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: I suppose manufactures encourage people to spend more by making them different colours

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: and designs.

cues.speaker: IE
cues.text: I'm sure when my parents bought their first fridge they had hardly any choice!
